title: Migration becomes a projection surface for urban insecurity when weak state capacity leaves jobs, housing, services, and belonging politically unresolved
source_unit: Konrad-Adenauer-Stiftung Occasional Paper Series No. 2/2026, Migration, Rule of Law, and Social Cohesion in Urban South Africa: Xenophobic Mobilisation as a Challenge to State Capacity
geography: Urban South Africa, focused on Gauteng/Johannesburg/Pretoria with Cape Town as a comparative context

denominator.unit: urban South African structural context examined in the qualitative study

official_unemployment.unit: percent official unemployment rate in South Africa in Q4 2025

expanded_unemployment.unit: percent expanded unemployment rate including discouraged work-seekers in Q4 2025

immigrant_population.unit: percent of population represented by more than three million immigrants in the report's cited 2026 context

structural_context.value: Migration intersects with unemployment, inequality, spatial segregation, informal work, limited public services, and institutional capacity constraints

causal_boundary.value: The report explicitly rejects migration as the sole or primary cause of unemployment or institutional overload

observations.method: Qualitative analysis of academic literature, policy reports, media coverage, public documents, and current South African migration, labor, and social-cohesion statistics.
observations.uncertainty: The study is not representative or comprehensive; the structural statistics provide context but do not identify the causal contribution of migration to unemployment, public-service pressure, or violence.
observations.subgroup: South African workers, African migrants, informal traders, urban residents, unemployed people, public-service users, and communities in Gauteng and Cape Town.
observations.counterinterpretation: Migration can support labor markets, household survival, and regional mobility; high unemployment and public-service strain may be driven primarily by domestic economic and institutional conditions.

observations.period: 1994-2026; xenophobic discrimination, violence, and social cohesion

denominator.unit: Xenowatch incident and impact series cited by the qualitative study

incidents.unit: xenophobic discrimination and violence incidents documented since 1994

displacements.unit: people displaced in the cited Xenowatch series

looted_businesses.unit: businesses looted in the cited Xenowatch series

deaths.unit: deaths in the cited Xenowatch series

violence_boundary.value: The study treats the figures as evidence that xenophobia is not merely transient attitude, while warning that under-reporting is likely

observations.method: Qualitative synthesis using Xenowatch, public reporting, research literature, and policy analysis.
observations.uncertainty: The series may undercount incidents and the study does not establish that all recorded harms are attributable to a single movement or cause; event definitions and reporting coverage matter.
observations.subgroup: African migrants, migrant-owned businesses, displaced residents, local communities, civil-society monitors, police, and public institutions.
observations.counterinterpretation: Documented incidents may be concentrated in high-visibility periods or locations; counter-mobilization and community solidarity can coexist with serious violence and exclusion.

observations.period: 2026; institutional trust, political attribution, and exclusionary mobilisation

denominator.unit: South African public-opinion and institutional-trust context synthesized in the study

parliament_trust.unit: approximately percent of the population reported as trusting parliament

political_party_trust.unit: percent of the population reported as trusting political parties

government_trust.unit: approximately percent of the population reported as trusting government

attribution_mechanism.value: When unemployment, housing, crime, service overload, and institutional failure are attributed to migrants, structural causes recede and conflict is reorganized around belonging and exclusion

private_authority.value: When public authorities appear overwhelmed or opaque, private movements can claim authority to verify residency, control access, or restore order

observations.method: Qualitative interpretation of Afrobarometer findings, media and political discourse, movement activity, and rule-of-law analysis.
observations.uncertainty: The study does not estimate a causal effect of trust on xenophobia or verify every cited public-opinion figure; political attribution varies across groups, locations, and time.
observations.subgroup: People with different socioeconomic capital, local residents, migrants, political movements, public agencies, and civil-society organizations.
observations.counterinterpretation: Public concern about migration can include legitimate questions about administrative capacity and legal status without necessarily producing xenophobic exclusion; low trust may be a consequence as well as a condition of mobilisation.

observations.period: 2022-2026; Gauteng and Cape Town urban variation

denominator.unit: urban contexts compared: Gauteng and Cape Town/Western Cape

gauteng_context.value: Gauteng concentrates labor-related migration, informal work, housing shortages, public-service competition, and visible organized xenophobic mobilisation

cape_town_context.value: Cape Town is more strongly associated in the study with spatial segregation, displacement, gentrification, housing and cost-of-living conflict, and less visible everyday exclusion

incident_comparison.value: The cited Xenowatch analysis recorded 79 incidents in Gauteng versus 36 in the Western Cape from 2022 to 2024

place_meaning.value: The same migration and belonging conflict takes different forms depending on labor markets, housing, spatial segregation, visibility, and institutional reach

observations.method: Qualitative comparison of urban contexts using migration, labor, housing, media, movement, and Xenowatch evidence.
observations.uncertainty: Two urban contexts cannot establish a general city typology; incident counts and qualitative contrasts may reflect differences in reporting, visibility, organization, or population scale.
observations.subgroup: Residents, internal and international migrants, informal workers, tenants, neighborhood organizations, city governments, and movements in Gauteng and the Western Cape.
observations.counterinterpretation: Organized visibility in Gauteng may make conflict appear more prevalent than everyday exclusion in Cape Town; urban differences may reflect institutional reporting rather than fundamentally different social dynamics.

related_sources.claim: Afrobarometer source cited for South African public attitudes toward immigration and foreigners.
Xenowatch source cited for documented incidents, displacement, business losses, and deaths.
Official 2026 qualitative paper and full methodological boundary.

boundary: This record adds a comparative urban-cohesion route from unemployment, inequality, housing, services, migration, and institutional distrust through political attribution, xenophobic mobilisation, rule-of-law erosion, private claims to authority, and social fragmentation. It is a qualitative case analysis with cited statistics and event series, not a representative public-opinion study, a causal migration-impact estimate, or a general claim about South Africa or migrants.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official Konrad-Adenauer-Stiftung PDF was reviewed for the South African labor and migration context, Xenowatch incident series, institutional trust, Gauteng/Cape Town comparison, and the paper's qualitative non-representative methodology.
